attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, endorsed.

semantics.note: Correctly separates the factual aside (syntax but not meaning, per Wolfram's benchmark) from the normative 'not the answer' recommendation. Unhedged present-tense claim.

contract.note: The plain reading treats 'meaning' as functional correctness alongside valid syntax in coding. That is an ordinary, fair reading. The July 2024 window fits 'new benchmark'.

evidence.note: Genuine June 2024 SAFIM preprint, but it covers a different benchmark and does not address Wolfram's results or the syntax-versus-meaning gap.

reviews.rationale: The packet contains no dated Wolfram benchmark results from July 2024 and no evaluation protocol. The only item is context about a different benchmark. The evidence available cannot establish or refute the claimed syntax/functionality gap or the attribution to Wolfram.

attribution.note: Marcus restates and endorses a point he co-authored in Rebooting AI and adds 'That hasn't really changed' in his own voice.

semantics.note: Keeps 'part of the reason', the 2019 baseline and the persistence claim. Causal kind is correct.

contract.note: Reading 'lack adequate techniques' as a persistent limitation in assurance and testing methods, not a total absence of techniques, is an ordinary and fair plain reading.

evidence.note: 2019 DeepMind research post: established testing and verification methods are hard to apply to deep learning, so new approaches are needed for robustness. It describes the field, not company self-promotion.
May 2024 IEEE Computer article: conventional structural coverage assurance transfers poorly to learned components, so the limitation persisted. It also shows partial progress.
2020 survey listing available ML engineering practices. It rules out a 'no techniques at all' reading but does not show the limitation was overcome.

reviews.rationale: e1 (2019) links the poor fit of established testing and verification methods to difficulty assuring robustness of ML systems. e2 (May 2024) documents the same kind of assurance limitation persisting. This meets the support condition. e3 and the progress noted in e2 do not show the limitation was substantially overcome. The evidence does not measure how much the limitation contributed to failures.
